messages.subject: Thesis abstract published
messages.body_plain:
Heya, BioGeoBEARS fans,

Happy New Year!  Finally got the (smallest!) piece of the thesis
published.  This was a thesis abstract published by Frontiers in
Biogeogeography.  It is open-access.  The figure is handy for
understanding the different models.

Reference: Matzke, Nicholas J. (2013). Probabilistic historical
biogeography: new models for founder-event speciation, imperfect
detection, and fossils allow improved accuracy and model-testing.
Frontiers of Biogeography, 5(4), 242-248.
http://escholarship.org/uc/item/44j7n141

Abstract

Historical biogeography has been characterized by a large diversity of
methods and unresolved debates about which processes, such as
dispersal or vicariance, are most important for explaining
distributions. A new R package, BioGeoBEARS, implements many models in
a common likelihood framework, so that standard statistical model
selection procedures can be applied to let the data choose the best
model. Available models include a likelihood version of DIVA
(“DIVALIKE”), LAGRANGE’s DEC model, and BAYAREA, as well as “+J”
versions of these models which include founder-event speciation, an
important process left out of most inference methods. I use
BioGeoBEARS on a large sample of island and non-island clades
(including two fossil clades) to show that founder-event speciation is
a crucial process in almost every clade, and that most published
datasets reject the non-J models currently in widespread use.
BioGeoBEARS is open-source and freely available for installation at
the Comprehensive R Archive Network at
http://CRAN.R-project.org/package=BioGeoBEARS. A step-by-step tutorial
is available at http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears.

Cheers!
Nick

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#toc0
====================================================
Update January 8, 2014: Fixes for optimx 2012 vs. optimx 2013 vs. optim() issues

During the January 7 workshop at the International Biogeography
Society Meeting in Canberra, Australia, some Windows users with new
versions of R were not able to install the 2012 version of optimx.
Switching to the R base function optim() worked, but caused a problem
with producing the graphics.

I have now fixed all of these problems in the revised example script,
posted below.  The script includes two source() commands which
contained revised functions.  Therefore, for the moment, begin all
BioGeoBEARS analyses with:

[[code]]
library(optimx)
library(BioGeoBEARS)
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_univ_model_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_plots_v1.R")
[[/code]]

As optimx is currently a dependency of BioGeoBEARS, you will still
need some version of optimx to get BioGeoBEARS to load.  I will make
it optional in the next big update.

I have tested the new example script using 2012 optimx, 2013 optimx,
and optim(), and all of them work. If you have problems, email me or
the BioGeoBEARS google group!
====================================================

Revised example script:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#toc11

Cheers, Nick

messages.subject_clean: BioGeoBEARS issues: Windows machines, small trees
messages.body_plain:
Hi group -- some recent answers, post-optimx fix:

Hi again! OK, I have a moment now... actually, do you mind if I post
these answers to the BioGeoBEARS google group?  This will help others
who have the same issue.

On Thu, Jan 16, 2014 at 12:52 AM,  X wrote:
> Dr. Matzke,
> I'm running BioGeoBEARS (pretty much that "out of the box" example with my
> data).
>
> I have a couple of questions:
>
>
> I'm getting quite different likelihoods if I run with "use_optimx=T" or "F".
> Something like -630 (when false) versus -920 (true). Do you have any idea
> about what might be going on?

This indicates the two Maximum Likelihood search optimizations are
finding different solutions.  I typically prefer optimx as it is
faster, but they should converge on the same result.  If the search is
hitting the limits of the parameters, though, then the search will
never find the optimum.  Hopefully, this will go away when the default
maximum values are adjusted, as below.

> The default maximum values for "d" and "e" are 5. I have to increase that a
> lot... I'm getting something like d=150, e=49. Should I be worried?? My tree
> has 120 tips and 8 areas.

This is fine.  It does mean that you probably have a very "short"
tree, with tiny branch lengths.  If you multiplied all of your
branches by 100 and saved this to a new Newick file, you would find that your optimal d and e parameters would then be 100 times smaller.

So, you can either rescale your tree, or raise the maximum value of d and e.  d and e are just
the "rate of the event per unit branch length", typically 5 is a good
max for a tree with a depth of 1 to 100, and units of millions of
years, but if you have a short tree you can change it.

(This logic only applies to the anagenetic parameters, not the
cladogenetic parameters.)

> As I said, I'm running the example. The first 5 models ran Ok (after I
> increased the maximum value), but the BAYAREAj is giving me an error:
>
> Error in calc_loglike_sp(tip_condlikes_of_data_on_each_state =
> tip_condlikes_of_data_on_each_state,  :
>   number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length
> However, it works if I run with use_optimx=T. Any idea?

This might mean that optim() is trying some value that produces a NaN
likelihood.  You could try adjusting the min/max values on the
parameters so that they are slightly further from 0 or 1 -- sometimes
the optimization seems to try values that are slightly beyond the
limits, even though I've set limits. Sometimes making the limits
tighter fixes things.

But, if it works with optimx, just use optimx.

Strangely, the error on the BayArea+J optimization run seems to happen only on Windows machines.  It may be some slight difference in how small numbers are treated, and some parameter value that is being tried during the search, that should be slightly above zero, is being rounded to 0 or a negative value.  This might be fixable by fiddling with the min for the variable parameters.

> If I use the source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--...... )  and more than
> one core, it gives me an error "cannot find detectCore function". With one
> core works fine.

For this, do
install.packages("parallel")
library(parallel)

...the newer versions of R come with parallel as a default, but
apparently this is not the case with Windows versions. Or, as you
found, just use one core.

Cheers!
Nick

>
> Thanks,
> Marcelo

messages.body_plain:
Alex agreed to let me post this answer concerning the number
of areas problem...thanks!

Nick

On 1/20/14 7:07 PM, Alex Pyron wrote:
 > Hi Nicholas,
 >
 >
 > I would really like to use BioGeoBEARS for a large-scale
 > dataset, and evaluate the alternative models (especially
 > founder-event speciation). My phylogeny [...] has 3309
taxa, divided among 12 major global
 > ecoregions. I realize that is a difficult problem to solve
 > in a DECj framework. I am experimenting with your tutorials
 > now, but I seem to primarily receive out-of-memory errors,
 > rather than satisfying results.
 >
 > What is a reasonable set of analysis dimensions and expected
 > runtimes? Is there anything special to be done with larger
 > datasets such as this? I will ultimately want to have
 > stratified connectivity matrices, etc. Any help you could
 > provide would be greatly appreciated.
 >
 >
 > Alex

-------- Original Message --------
Subject: Re: BioGeoBEARS runtime dimensions
Date: Mon, 20 Jan 2014 19:28:20 -0500
From: Nick Matzke <mat...@berkeley.edu>
Reply-To: mat...@berkeley.edu
To: Alex Pyron <rpy...@colubroid.org>

Hi Alex! I'm a fan of your work!

Can I post this answer to the BioGeoBEARS google group?
This makes it easier for the next person with a similar
question.

(also, I can add you to the group if you like)

The problem here is the number of areas.

12 areas equals...

= 2^12 possible combinations of presence/absence in each area

= 2^12 states = 4096 "states" (think of a character with
4096 states, that's what BioGeoBEARS/LAGRANGE are doing)

= a transition matrix of 4096x4096

= 16,777,216 cells in the transition matrix that have to be
stored just to represent the matrix in memory.

Then the matrix has to be exponentiated to calculate
likelihoods on the branches.

In my experience, if transition matrices get bigger than
about 550x550, the matrix exponentiation takes >1 second per
exponentiation, which means a tree with 100 branches takes
>100 seconds per likelihood calculation, which means
slooooow for a maximum likelihood search.

With a really zippy computer you might do a little better,
but I think matrix exponentiation is quadratic or worse with
# of states.

It would be even slower with 3309 taxa, but speed should be
linear with # of taxa, the problem is the matrix size.

Options:

1. Reduce the size of the state space by limiting the
maximum # of areas.  Use:

numstates_from_numareas(12, 12)
numstates_from_numareas(12, 3)

...to see how this works.

This is defensible especially if no species lives in e.g.
more than 3 areas.  One could also manually list all desired
states, all this would take is some R skillz.

2. Try the sparse matrix exponetiation routines with
use_sparse=TRUE.  Theoretically, sparse matrix routines can
handle much bigger matrices.  I implemented this in
rexpokit, but haven't had much luck, the calculations that
result appear to be more approximate, so in an ML search I
get different answers. In a Bayesian analysis maybe it would
be OK.  You/we would probably have to tweak the BioGeoBEARS
functions manually since I didn't implement all the
corresponding calculations for sparse matrices in BioGeoBEARS.

3. Use the BayArea C++ program, realizing that it has no
cladogenesis model and my model testing suggests that this
is almost always very poorly performing compared to e.g.
DEC+J in terms of AIC etc.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject_clean: BioGeoBEARS max_areas, ancestral states, plotting control parameters
messages.body_plain:
Answers to some questions:

On 1/22/14 11:04 PM, Alex Pyron wrote:
> Hi Nick,
>
>
> If you'd prefer me to move this to the group instead of
> bugging you directly, please let me know. I tried to find
> the answers in the current documentation; apologies if I
> overlooked something. A few questions:
>
> 1) It seems that you *must* have the max number of areas
> equal to that observed in the extant taxa. Is this the case?
> For me it fails when the max is greater.

Theoretically, if your geography data is e.g.:

3309	8	(A B C D E F G H)
sp1	11000000
sp2	00000010
...etc...

It should work for anything from 2 to 8 areas (or,
hopefully, 1 to 8 areas, but I haven't extensively tested 1
area, which might require re-parameterization).

The number of states in the transition matrix is much bigger
for max_range_size = 8:

numstates_from_numareas(8,2)
36

numstates_from_numareas(8,8)
255

...so perhaps you are hitting some memory issue with the
larger matrix?  I wouldn't necessarily think so, (3309
species + 3308 internal nodes) * 255 possible states isn't
THAT big a data table (1687335 cells).

In the Psychotria example, you can see that the default
allows species to live in up to 4 areas, even though each
individual species is observed in only 1 area.

Sometimes, particular configurations of allowed areas and
constraints can result in 0 likelihood (-Inf log-likelihood)
for certain parameter values, which can crash the ML search.
The solution is usually to tweak the min/max values for the
parameters, and/or change 0 to e.g. 0.0000001 in e.g. the
probability multiplier constraint matrix.

> 2) How exactly do we interpret the node/branch labels? At
> first I thought that the node simply showed the two states
> descended from that node, and that the label on the base of
> the branch was the state for that branch. However, I see
> some cases in which the label on a node is not simply the
> upper and lower states, and is different from the label at
> the base of the branch. What changes are possible along
> branches and at nodes?

So, the labels/pie charts AT the nodes represent the states
(states = geographic ranges) at the branch TOPS,
infinitesimally before the "instantaneous" speciation event.

The labels/pie charts at the "corners" on the phylogeny,
i.e. the branch bottoms, represent the states at the branch
BOTTOMS, i.e. infinitessimally AFTER the "instantaneous"
speciation event.

These are distinguished, because in the
LAGRANGE/BioGeoBEARS-type biogeography models, unlike most
evolutionary models, special processes happen
instantaneously at speciation.

Some versions/settings of LAGRANGE seem to report the joint
probabilities of (ancestor, left descendant, right
descendant) range inheritance scenarios.  I didn't do this,
because it is harder to keep track of, and harder to parse
afterwards, and I'm not sure what it accomplishes, since
most people care mostly about the states.

BioGeoBEARS by default reports ancestral state probabilities
under the globally optimum model. This is different than
what LAGRANGE does (local optimization). Local optimization
can be done in BioGeoBEARS, but you have to write a for-loop
and use the fixnode option.

These are both different than finding the "single best joint
history".  For the different types of ancestral states, see
the Matzke 2013 Ph.D. thesis and Felsenstein (2004).

The upshot is that the best states at each node in
BioGeoBEARS or LAGRANGE cannot always be read exactly as a
consistent joint history.  However, finding the single best
joint history is nontrivial, and even if found, it might
have a tiny probability compared to all other possible
histories.

For more, see:

1. BIOGEOBEARS VS LAGRANGE ANCESTRAL STATES
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/ancestral$20state/biogeobears/LlbN1jW8w5E/TxqZZuX6d3sJ

> 3) Is there a simple way to get a LAGRANGE-like output,
> where the potential states are listed for every node, ranked
> by relative probability (or likelihood, or AIC weight,
> whatever)? Presumably this will be needed for publication,
> to report exact values.

Yes, see:

2. NODE NUMBERS IN R / BIOGEOBEARS FOR ANCESTRAL STATES
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/ancestral$20state/biogeobears/LlbN1jW8w5E/TxqZZuX6d3sJ

E.g.:

resDEC$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node

In this table, the rows correspond to the APE node numbers,
and the columns correspond to each possible ancestral
state=each possible geographic range.

The plot_BioGeoBEARS_results() function just extracts these
probabilities from the resDEC object (or resDECj or
whatever) to plot either the best single state, or the pie
charts of all states.

IMPORTANT NOTES:

A. Phylogeny node numbers are ALL DIFFERENT (sigh!) in the
output of:

APE/BioGeoBEARS
DIVA
Python LAGRANGE
C++ LAGRANGE.

See get_lagrange_nodenums() and
postorder_nodes_phylo4_return_table().

B. WHEN THERE ARE TIES FOR THE MOST PROBABLE STATE, THE
*FIRST* STATE (leftmost column in e.g.
resDEC$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node)
IS CHOSEN FOR PLOTTING.  This can make some history plots
look odd.

This decision was made to avoid crashes that were occuring
when there were ties.  Look at the pie charts to see when
this is the case.

> 4) Where are the control parameters for plotting the
> phylogeny? I need to reduce the tip and branch labels, and
> pie charts. I also need to make a longer PDF file, but it
> fails when I set height over 200.

As you can see from the example:

res1 = plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object,
analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("j"), plotwhat="text",
label.offset=0.45, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6,
titlecex=0.8, plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir,
include_null_range=TRUE, tr=tr, tipranges=tipranges)

...the control paramters are the "...cex" parameters in
plot_BioGeoBEARS_results().  cex refers character expansion,
as with other R plotting (I use it for the pie charts etc. too).

If I didn't cover everything, you might have to make a
custom version of plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(), call it
plot_BioGeoBEARS_results2(), and source it.

plot_BioGeoBEARS_results() mostly just accesses the standard
APE plotting functions, so it shouldn't be too hard to
figure out.

 > I also need to make a longer PDF file, but it
 > fails when I set height over 200.

You have a huge tree, so there might not be an easy solution
to getting it all to look nice.  With some R skillz the tree
could be split up, as well as the
resDEC$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node;
this would have to track the original versus new node numbers.

Re: max number of inches in the PDF.  Did you increase the
width as well?  There might be some absolute limit
regardless?  I hear there are alternatives to pdf() for
plotting, but I can't remember what they are.  You can also
comment out #pdf() and thus plot to screen, and then save to
whatever format.

> 5) How would you philosophically interpret the
> reconstruction of single areas from time periods where they
> were accreted? For instance, I'm getting firm "Nearctic"
> reconstructions with multiple "dispersals" into the
> Palearctic prior to the breakup of Laurasia.

The interpretation would depend on the other constraints, if
any...BioGeoBEARS by default just thinks of each individual
area as a 1 or a 0, occupied or not, with all areas
"equidistant"/equally connected, unless you've given it
information about connectivity or distance.

I'm happy to take a look if you like.

> All of these questions pertain to the settings as given in
> the out-of-the-box /Psychotria/ example, adapted to my data.
> I've got it running for 8 areas (2 max) with 3309 taxa.
> Thanks!!! I love BioGeoBEARS!!!

Awesome!  Glad it's basically working!!

Cheers, Nick

Answers to some questions:

On 1/22/14 11:04 PM, Alex Pyron wrote:
> Hi Nick,
>
>
> If you'd prefer me to move this to the group instead of
> bugging you directly, please let me know. I tried to find
> the answers in the current documentation; apologies if I
> overlooked something. A few questions:
>
> 1) It seems that you *must* have the max number of areas
> equal to that observed in the extant taxa. Is this the case?
> For me it fails when the max is greater.

Theoretically, if your geography data is e.g.:

3309    8       (A B C D E F G H)
sp1     11000000
sp2     00000010
...etc...

It should work for anything from 2 to 8 areas (or,
hopefully, 1 to 8 areas, but I haven't extensively tested 1
area, which might require re-parameterization).

The number of states in the transition matrix is much bigger
for max_range_size = 8:

numstates_from_numareas(8,2)
36

numstates_from_numareas(8,8)
255

...so perhaps you are hitting some memory issue with the
larger matrix?  I wouldn't necessarily think so, (3309
species + 3308 internal nodes) * 255 possible states isn't
THAT big a data table (1687335 cells).

In the Psychotria example, you can see that the default
allows species to live in up to 4 areas, even though each
individual species is observed in only 1 area.

Sometimes, particular configurations of allowed areas and
constraints can result in 0 likelihood (-Inf log-likelihood)
for certain parameter values, which can crash the ML search.
The solution is usually to tweak the min/max values for the
parameters, and/or change 0 to e.g. 0.0000001 in e.g. the
probability multiplier constraint matrix.

> 2) How exactly do we interpret the node/branch labels? At
> first I thought that the node simply showed the two states
> descended from that node, and that the label on the base of
> the branch was the state for that branch. However, I see
> some cases in which the label on a node is not simply the
> upper and lower states, and is different from the label at
> the base of the branch. What changes are possible along
> branches and at nodes?

So, the labels/pie charts AT the nodes represent the states
(states = geographic ranges) at the branch TOPS,
infinitesimally before the "instantaneous" speciation event.

The labels/pie charts at the "corners" on the phylogeny,
i.e. the branch bottoms, represent the states at the branch
BOTTOMS, i.e. infinitessimally AFTER the "instantaneous"
speciation event.

These are distinguished, because in the
LAGRANGE/BioGeoBEARS-type biogeography models, unlike most
evolutionary models, special processes happen
instantaneously at speciation.

Some versions/settings of LAGRANGE seem to report the joint
probabilities of (ancestor, left descendant, right
descendant) range inheritance scenarios.  I didn't do this,
because it is harder to keep track of, and harder to parse
afterwards, and I'm not sure what it accomplishes, since
most people care mostly about the states.

BioGeoBEARS by default reports ancestral state probabilities
under the globally optimum model. This is different than
what LAGRANGE does (local optimization). Local optimization
can be done in BioGeoBEARS, but you have to write a for-loop
and use the fixnode option.

These are both different than finding the "single best joint
history".  For the different types of ancestral states, see
the Matzke 2013 Ph.D. thesis and Felsenstein (2004).

The upshot is that the best states at each node in
BioGeoBEARS or LAGRANGE cannot always be read exactly as a
consistent joint history.  However, finding the single best
joint history is nontrivial, and even if found, it might
have a tiny probability compared to all other possible
histories.

For more, see:

1. BIOGEOBEARS VS LAGRANGE ANCESTRAL STATES
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/ancestral$20state/biogeobears/LlbN1jW8w5E/TxqZZuX6d3sJ

> 3) Is there a simple way to get a LAGRANGE-like output,
> where the potential states are listed for every node, ranked
> by relative probability (or likelihood, or AIC weight,
> whatever)? Presumably this will be needed for publication,
> to report exact values.

Yes, see:

2. NODE NUMBERS IN R / BIOGEOBEARS FOR ANCESTRAL STATES
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/ancestral$20state/biogeobears/LlbN1jW8w5E/TxqZZuX6d3sJ

E.g.:

resDEC$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node

In this table, the rows correspond to the APE node numbers,
and the columns correspond to each possible ancestral
state=each possible geographic range.

The plot_BioGeoBEARS_results() function just extracts these
probabilities from the resDEC object (or resDECj or
whatever) to plot either the best single state, or the pie
charts of all states.

IMPORTANT NOTES:

A. Phylogeny node numbers are ALL DIFFERENT (sigh!) in the
output of:

APE/BioGeoBEARS
DIVA
Python LAGRANGE
C++ LAGRANGE.

See get_lagrange_nodenums() and
postorder_nodes_phylo4_return_table().

B. WHEN THERE ARE TIES FOR THE MOST PROBABLE STATE, THE
*FIRST* STATE (leftmost column in e.g.
resDEC$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node)
IS CHOSEN FOR PLOTTING.  This can make some history plots
look odd.

This decision was made to avoid crashes that were occuring
when there were ties.  Look at the pie charts to see when
this is the case.

> 4) Where are the control parameters for plotting the
> phylogeny? I need to reduce the tip and branch labels, and
> pie charts. I also need to make a longer PDF file, but it
> fails when I set height over 200.

As you can see from the example:

res1 = plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object,
analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("j"), plotwhat="text",
label.offset=0.45, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6,
titlecex=0.8, plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir,
include_null_range=TRUE, tr=tr, tipranges=tipranges)

...the control paramters are the "...cex" parameters in
plot_BioGeoBEARS_results().  cex refers character expansion,
as with other R plotting (I use it for the pie charts etc. too).

If I didn't cover everything, you might have to make a
custom version of plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(), call it
plot_BioGeoBEARS_results2(), and source it.

plot_BioGeoBEARS_results() mostly just accesses the standard
APE plotting functions, so it shouldn't be too hard to
figure out.

 > I also need to make a longer PDF file, but it
 > fails when I set height over 200.

You have a huge tree, so there might not be an easy solution
to getting it all to look nice.  With some R skillz the tree
could be split up, as well as the
resDEC$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node;
this would have to track the original versus new node numbers.

Re: max number of inches in the PDF.  Did you increase the
width as well?  There might be some absolute limit
regardless?  I hear there are alternatives to pdf() for
plotting, but I can't remember what they are.  You can also
comment out #pdf() and thus plot to screen, and then save to
whatever format.

> 5) How would you philosophically interpret the
> reconstruction of single areas from time periods where they
> were accreted? For instance, I'm getting firm "Nearctic"
> reconstructions with multiple "dispersals" into the
> Palearctic prior to the breakup of Laurasia.

The interpretation would depend on the other constraints, if
any...BioGeoBEARS by default just thinks of each individual
area as a 1 or a 0, occupied or not, with all areas
"equidistant"/equally connected, unless you've given it
information about connectivity or distance.

I'm happy to take a look if you like.

> Thanks!!! I love BioGeoBEARS!!!

Awesome!  Glad it's basically working!!

> On 1/22/14 11:04 PM, Alex Pyron wrote:
>> Hi Nick,
>>
>>
>> If you'd prefer me to move this to the group instead of
>> bugging you directly, please let me know. I tried to find
>> the answers in the current documentation; apologies if I
>> overlooked something. A few questions:
>>
>> 1) It seems that you *must* have the max number of areas
>> equal to that observed in the extant taxa. Is this the case?
>> For me it fails when the max is greater.
>
> Theoretically, if your geography data is e.g.:
>
> 3309    8       (A B C D E F G H)
> sp1     11000000
> sp2     00000010
> ...etc...
>
> It should work for anything from 2 to 8 areas (or,
> hopefully, 1 to 8 areas, but I haven't extensively tested 1
> area, which might require re-parameterization).
>
> The number of states in the transition matrix is much bigger
> for max_range_size = 8:
>
> numstates_from_numareas(8,2)
> 36
>
> numstates_from_numareas(8,8)
> 255
>
> ...so perhaps you are hitting some memory issue with the
> larger matrix?  I wouldn't necessarily think so, (3309
> species + 3308 internal nodes) * 255 possible states isn't
> THAT big a data table (1687335 cells).
>
> In the Psychotria example, you can see that the default
> allows species to live in up to 4 areas, even though each
> individual species is observed in only 1 area.
>
> Sometimes, particular configurations of allowed areas and
> constraints can result in 0 likelihood (-Inf log-likelihood)
> for certain parameter values, which can crash the ML search.
> The solution is usually to tweak the min/max values for the
> parameters, and/or change 0 to e.g. 0.0000001 in e.g. the
> probability multiplier constraint matrix.
>
>
>
>> 2) How exactly do we interpret the node/branch labels? At
>> first I thought that the node simply showed the two states
>> descended from that node, and that the label on the base of
>> the branch was the state for that branch. However, I see
>> some cases in which the label on a node is not simply the
>> upper and lower states, and is different from the label at
>> the base of the branch. What changes are possible along
>> branches and at nodes?
>
>
> So, the labels/pie charts AT the nodes represent the states
> (states = geographic ranges) at the branch TOPS,
> infinitesimally before the "instantaneous" speciation event.
>
> The labels/pie charts at the "corners" on the phylogeny,
> i.e. the branch bottoms, represent the states at the branch
> BOTTOMS, i.e. infinitessimally AFTER the "instantaneous"
> speciation event.
>
> These are distinguished, because in the
> LAGRANGE/BioGeoBEARS-type biogeography models, unlike most
> evolutionary models, special processes happen
> instantaneously at speciation.
>
> Some versions/settings of LAGRANGE seem to report the joint
> probabilities of (ancestor, left descendant, right
> descendant) range inheritance scenarios.  I didn't do this,
> because it is harder to keep track of, and harder to parse
> afterwards, and I'm not sure what it accomplishes, since
> most people care mostly about the states.
>
> BioGeoBEARS by default reports ancestral state probabilities
> under the globally optimum model. This is different than
> what LAGRANGE does (local optimization). Local optimization
> can be done in BioGeoBEARS, but you have to write a for-loop
> and use the fixnode option.
>
> These are both different than finding the "single best joint
> history".  For the different types of ancestral states, see
> the Matzke 2013 Ph.D. thesis and Felsenstein (2004).
>
> The upshot is that the best states at each node in
> BioGeoBEARS or LAGRANGE cannot always be read exactly as a
> consistent joint history.  However, finding the single best
> joint history is nontrivial, and even if found, it might
> have a tiny probability compared to all other possible
> histories.
>
> For more, see:
>
> 1. BIOGEOBEARS VS LAGRANGE ANCESTRAL STATES
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/ancestral$20state/biogeobears/LlbN1jW8w5E/TxqZZuX6d3sJ
>
>
>
>> 3) Is there a simple way to get a LAGRANGE-like output,
>> where the potential states are listed for every node, ranked
>> by relative probability (or likelihood, or AIC weight,
>> whatever)? Presumably this will be needed for publication,
>> to report exact values.
>
>
> Yes, see:
>
> 2. NODE NUMBERS IN R / BIOGEOBEARS FOR ANCESTRAL STATES
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/ancestral$20state/biogeobears/LlbN1jW8w5E/TxqZZuX6d3sJ
>
> E.g.:
>
> resDEC$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node
>
> In this table, the rows correspond to the APE node numbers,
> and the columns correspond to each possible ancestral
> state=each possible geographic range.
>
> The plot_BioGeoBEARS_results() function just extracts these
> probabilities from the resDEC object (or resDECj or
> whatever) to plot either the best single state, or the pie
> charts of all states.
>
>
> IMPORTANT NOTES:
>
> A. Phylogeny node numbers are ALL DIFFERENT (sigh!) in the
> output of:
>
> APE/BioGeoBEARS
> DIVA
> Python LAGRANGE
> C++ LAGRANGE.
>
> See get_lagrange_nodenums() and
> postorder_nodes_phylo4_return_table().
>
>
> B. WHEN THERE ARE TIES FOR THE MOST PROBABLE STATE, THE
> *FIRST* STATE (leftmost column in e.g.
> resDEC$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node)
> IS CHOSEN FOR PLOTTING.  This can make some history plots
> look odd.
>
> This decision was made to avoid crashes that were occuring
> when there were ties.  Look at the pie charts to see when
> this is the case.
>
>
>
>> 4) Where are the control parameters for plotting the
>> phylogeny? I need to reduce the tip and branch labels, and
>> pie charts. I also need to make a longer PDF file, but it
>> fails when I set height over 200.
>
> As you can see from the example:
>
> res1 = plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object,
> analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("j"), plotwhat="text",
> label.offset=0.45, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6,
> titlecex=0.8, plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir,
> include_null_range=TRUE, tr=tr, tipranges=tipranges)
>
> ...the control paramters are the "...cex" parameters in
> plot_BioGeoBEARS_results().  cex refers character expansion,
> as with other R plotting (I use it for the pie charts etc. too).
>
> If I didn't cover everything, you might have to make a
> custom version of plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(), call it
> plot_BioGeoBEARS_results2(), and source it.
>
> plot_BioGeoBEARS_results() mostly just accesses the standard
> APE plotting functions, so it shouldn't be too hard to
> figure out.
>
>
>
>
>   > I also need to make a longer PDF file, but it
>   > fails when I set height over 200.
>
>
> You have a huge tree, so there might not be an easy solution
> to getting it all to look nice.  With some R skillz the tree
> could be split up, as well as the
> resDEC$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node;
> this would have to track the original versus new node numbers.
>
> Re: max number of inches in the PDF.  Did you increase the
> width as well?  There might be some absolute limit
> regardless?  I hear there are alternatives to pdf() for
> plotting, but I can't remember what they are.  You can also
> comment out #pdf() and thus plot to screen, and then save to
> whatever format.
>
>
>

>> reconstruction of single areas from time periods where they
>> were accreted? For instance, I'm getting firm "Nearctic"
>> reconstructions with multiple "dispersals" into the
>> Palearctic prior to the breakup of Laurasia.

Hi Marcelo,

On 1/30/14 4:20 PM, regin...@yahoo.com.br wrote:

>     think that make sense to use BioGeoBEARS to test
>     different area schemes (same number of areas, different
>     boundaries, or even different number of areas,
>     etc...)... that would be using the same model, same
>     group, same phylogeny... or doesn't?

The difficult thing here is that likelihoods can only be
compared between different models on the *same* tip data.
Changing the definition of the geographic regions in effect
changes the geography data at the tips.

Likelihood means "probability of the data given a model",
where the "model" means "phylogeny + geographic evolution
model + model parameters".

So, using the same data, you could compare the likelihood of
the data using different trees, different geographic
evolution models, different model parameters, etc.  But
changing the regions changes the data, at least in this
"discrete biogeography" way of doing things.

There may be some way around this by building a hiearchical
model, but I haven't thought about it much.  Defining
"discrete regions" is very often the biggest judgment call
in these sort of analyses!  When the clade lives on islands,
it's pretty simple. On continents, people often use
ecoregions, elevational zones, etc.

A number of recent biogeography papers on South America have
used about the same ecoregions, maybe you could use a subset
of those?  See e.g. the Taygetis biogeography paper (google
those words to find it, I forget the reference).

What *is* feasible is to have the same areas, but have them
connected, or not, in different ways, have different
dispersal multipliers, different distances, etc., and
compare all those different models.

>     "bears_9param_standard_fast_ys_v_cb"? The help files are
>     the same and I guess the function also (as far as I
>     could tell).

Actually, I'm going to delete those functions at some point,
they are shortcuts to some models I was playing with.
"bears_6param_standard_fast_ys_v" should work.  I'm not sure
about "bears_9param_standard_fast_ys_v_cb", a model with 9
free parameters is even crazier than a model with 6!

bears_optim_run(), which you run with:

messages.subject: BioGeoBEARS IMPORTANT BUG FIX
messages.body_plain:
Hi all BioGeoBEARS users,

I recently noticed, and fixed, a bug in the uppass
calculations, which are important for calculating ancestral
state probabilities.  Sometimes, certain probabilities were
being overwritten rather than added during the calculations.

This fix may resolve certain cases where "contradictory"
node states and corner states were observed. (Other cases
may be probability ties — check the pie charts — or due to
the fact that ancestral states under the global ML model are
not the same thing as a single coherent history; see joint
ancestral states, Felsenstein 2004, for that sort of
estimation method).

The bug fix will not change the estimation of ancestral
state probabilities at the root, nor the likelihood
calculations for different models, as these only involve
downpass calculations.

The downpass calculations also dominate the ancestral state
probabilities for most nodes, so most ancestral state
probabilities won't change much.  However, especially at the
branches attaching to the root, the bug fix may make a
difference.  I have run the fixed calculations on a few
datasets and not noticed huge differences.

However, I strongly recommend everyone re-run their
ancestral state analyses with the fix.  For now, after every
time where your script says "library(BioGeoBEARS)", add
these two lines:

================================
library(BioGeoBEARS)

source("http://phylo.wikidot.com/local--files/biogeobears/calc_loglike_sp_v01.R")

calc_loglike_sp = compiler::cmpfun(calc_loglike_sp_prebyte)
================================

I have also edited the example script, at PhyloWiki, and put
a note there:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#toc0

Thanks very much,

Nick Matzke

> Also, I understand the d and e values from the global optimization because
> they are based on branch lengths, changes over unit time, but what does the
> j value of the global optimization mean, what does it represent? Is it the
> probability of a founder event per node, so its not a rate, right?
>
> Thanks for the feedback and take care!

Hi!

j, and the other parameters y, s, and v (usually hidden) are the
"per-event weights".  If j=y=s=v =1, then all of the events have equal
weight, on a per-event basis.  In DEC+J, j ranges from 0-3, and y,s,v
each have weight (3-j)/3.

The tricky bit is that there are different possible numbers of events,
conditional on each different ancestral range.

Basically, though, the weights get added up and divided by the total
to produce the conditional probability of any particular event
conditional on any particular ancestral range.

calculations for DEC and DEC+J by hand: PDF caption -- Excel file

Cheers!

Hi,

'clusterApply' is a function for farming out a repeated calculation to
multiple cores.  In BioGeoBEARS, I enable this for the matrix
exponentiation on branches. It helps speed a lot when you have lots of
areas and branches, and thus slow calculation of likelihoods.  E.g.
use of 4 cores may be 4 times faster. It doesn't matter much, or may
even be slower, for small problems like the Psychotria dataset.

That can be fixed with library(snow) or library(parallel).  It only
matters if you are doing multicore processing.

I believe that parallel functions cause a crash in the Mac R.app, so
bears_optim_run() will switch things to single-core in R.app.

I think in R 3.0, the parallel library is part of R base on Macs, but
this doesn't seem to be the case on PCs. In any case, library(snow) or
(parallel) should fix this warning.

Cheers!
Nick
